chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Basir, who said:
Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'If a man were to strike a man with pottery, or with a brick, or with a plank of wood, and he died, it would be a deliberate (killing).'

key_terms.آجُرَّة: Brick — a fired clay construction material, similarly capable of causing death when used as a weapon
key_terms.خَزَفَة: Pottery/potsherd — a piece of fired clay, not typically considered a weapon but capable of lethal use
key_terms.عَمْد: Deliberate/intentional — the legal category of intentional homicide in Islamic jurisprudence, triggering qisas (retaliation)
key_terms.عُود: Plank/stick of wood — a generic wooden object, used here to illustrate that the material need not be a conventional weapon

ai.seo_question: Does striking someone with pottery, a brick, or wood that causes death count as deliberate killing in Islamic law?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) rules that striking someone with objects such as pottery shards, bricks, or wooden planks, resulting in death, constitutes deliberate (intentional) homicide — qatl al-'amd — even though these are not conventional weapons. This ruling is significant in Islamic jurisprudence because it extends the definition of 'amd (deliberateness) beyond weaponized killing to any act where a normally lethal instrument is used with lethal outcome. The Imam's audience — legal students and companions seeking precise jurisprudential boundaries — would have understood this as defining the threshold for qisas (retaliation) liability.
